These things are imposed upon us by bureaucrats, Mr. Speaker, which has the reputation for trying to control and regulate everybody. It does not help at all to impose these silly things upon us, but, Mr. Speaker, we do want to be completely metric. I know that we must change some of our terminology and keep up with the times.
As a young lad I remember, when out hunting in the bush with older men, that one of the older fellows in the party got a little warm and said, "Across that ridge, about a mile away over the hill in the bush, there is a Swedish chap who is homesteading. Let's visit him." We climbed over the ridge and went to the homesteader's shack. One of the older men in the party said to the Swedish lad, a great, tall, burly, blonde-headed giant, "Oily, have you got a crock?" Oily looked him squarely in the eye and said, "I don't know what's the matter with you Canadians I came to this country 15 years ago and it took me 15 years to learn to say a jug'"-he pronounced it with a "Y", "yug"-"and now you call it a crock."
I am trying to make my point, clear with this illustration. We must change from "yug" to "crock"-at least we must make such changes occasionally. But, for heaven's sake, take it easy on the poor guy on the production side of the economy who is trying to sell his product in a convenient and profitable fashion.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin my remarks in this totally non-partisan debate by suggesting that the government should consider some of the sensible suggestions made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). If the exceptions he suggested were made, I do not think the implementation, in principle, of the metric system would suffer.
I think most members of this House can see the value of the metric system. It is a simple system, based on multiples of ten, and is used in many countries of the world. Basically, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain summed up the feelings of many people who come from the prairies about the difficulties the metric system will cause, particularly to the farmers of this country. Our farmers will need to learn the new system. However, I do not foresee any great economic advantage which will accrue to our farmers and to society from the difficulties and torment of learning the new system. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain noted, we shall not sell more wheat just because we adopt a new system. The adoption of this bill as it applies to farmers will facilitate matters somewhat for international companies trading in grain and the like. But it probably will not help us sell more grain. If the government is serious about selling more grain, it should talk seriously to governments around the world about reviving the International Grains Agreement which lapsed, so far as this country is concerned, several years ago.

We shall feel the effects in the next few weeks of the lack of such an agreement when we witness how the price of grain on world markets fluctuates according to the whim of speculators. The price will not be governed by any kind of rational pricing system or agreement. Surely it would be better to enact measures which would facilitate exports and trade, instead of fooling around with the metric system.
Our farmers face some very real problems involving the metric system. As has been said before, farms on the prairies have been surveyed: we have talked of farms in terms of square miles, sections of land, quarter sections, and so on. We have townships, correctional lines, sections, and the like. We have used such measurements deliberately and carefully over the years. Those measurements form part of the culture, not just of the farmers in western Canada but of all the people, particularly those on the prairies. Changing such a system will mean a great deal of difficulty for individual farmers and, as well, much additional cost for all farmers and society as a whole.
I should like the minister responsible to tell the House how much our metric conversion will cost the farmers of this country. How much will the total conversion cost? Can anyone estimate what the cost will be to the public treasury? I think we should be concerned about cost, in our capacity as parliamentarians. We must ask if this bill will bring to the people of Canada tangible benefits, or will the cost of conversion outweigh the benefits? I am thinking particularly of the farming segment when I say that. Will it be worthwhile for farmers? As others have said, conversion will create great anxieties and problems for farmers. Many farmers have approached me and said, "If the new system is adopted in the spring, how will I adjust my seeders and drills? When I go to seed my crop, how will I adjust my drill to seed in hectares, since the drill has been set up to seed by the acre?" Perhaps the minister can explain to the farmers of western Canada what they ought to do. I am not being political; I am merely repeating something which I as a member from western Canada have heard time and again from farmers of all political stripes.
Let me raise some further points of concern. If the farmer is to deal in hectares, how will he know how much fertilizer to put on his land, since he has been used to dealing in acres? Or how will he know how much chemical spray to use for any given number of hectares? These are questions of real difficulty for farmers. If the farmer buys land, how can he judge how many hectares will fit, say, into a quarter section? Our whole system of measurements will go through a radical change. I suspect that farmers, more than any other group in society, will be affected in a practical way by the changeover to the metric system. They are concerned about the coming change.
Some farmers can visualize the benefits of the new system. For instance farmers, as well as others, can see the benefits of the adoption of the Celsius system with respect to temperature. We all know that changes must come, and do not argue the point. However, farmers will face all kinds of practical problems with the changeover. They will face effects which may be
Metric System
completely different to those affecting the rest of us as we change over to the metric system. We shall need to become accustomed to thinking in terms of hectares instead of acres, kilometres instead of miles, litres instead of gallons, and the like. As well, the farmer must deal with his tools and educate himself about the various sizes of tools he needs to repair farm machinery or perform other functions on the farm. Clearly, farmers face some very real difficulties.
May I make a suggestion? If the government is not in favour of providing certain exemptions, as suggested, let it at least provide some program of education for farmers and some program of assistance and compensation whereby farmers could be compensated for some of the economic losses they will endure. One cannot compensate farmers for all the agony and torment they will go through in learning the new system, but one can compensate them for the economic loss they will suffer. I appeal to the government to consider allowing some of the exemptions which have been suggested.
Speaking personally, from my somewhat limited knowledge of farming I suggest that if we could exempt certain aspects of farming we would make conditions a great deal easier for farmers and farm products for the country would probably be cheaper. That would still not hinder the implementation of the metric system in this country. Surely that is the least we can do as parliamentarians.
My last point is this. I have the impression, which is not wrong, I think, that farm organizations and municipalities across the prairies-indeed, right across Canada-have not been adequately canvassed and consulted about the effects of metric conversion. I think the government ought to pause a moment, ought to consult farm organizations, rural municipalities and other affected communities and ask what they think about the government's program. Let it ask them for suggestions which might change the program without hurting the principle of what the government is trying to achieve in the long run. I do not think that would hurt the government and it would not hurt the process of metric conversion. I do not think you can impose something like this upon the people of this country and expect them to sit idly by like sheep or puppets.
We have a lot of problems in this country. Many are caused by governments and bureaucrats making decisions in offices without any comprehension of what the result of the decision will be on the farm or in the factory. The implementation of something like this may seem a little thing to city people. They say, "Can't the farmer convert something from an acre to a hectare?" That is the attitude of a lot of people. If you keep making decisions like that, how can you expect the people to have any real pride in Canadianism, a fervour to do something for the country, or a spirit of commitment? How can you expect the people of this country to be productive and pull together like people in some other countries if you constantly put obstacles of this sort in their path?
If we were to create some difficulties that in the end would help the people, I am sure they would understand. However,

January 26, 1977
Metric System
doing something like this will not build up their morale. It will not make the farm population more productive, nor will it make them more enthusiastic Canadians. They will not have any more love for Ottawa, federal institutions and federal structures at a time when this is badly needed. The government could get around part of this by pausing at this time, going to the prairies and saying, "This is what we plan". They should consult the people there. There should be input from farm organizations and local governments. The government should honestly be open to some changes in possible exemptions, or perhaps a longer staging of the implementation of the metric system. If the government went there with that openness and willingness to listen, the people of rural, western Canada would be very happy and gratified.
We need that type of thing. People must genuinely feel that federal institutions are working on their behalf, working with them and not doing things to them. Too many people believe that the federal government and eastern Canada are doing things to them because of all the inequities in this country. Without rambling on, I plead once more for the government to take a second look at some parts of this bill as it pertains to western agriculture, with a view to having input from the farmers and others who are affected. They should look seriously, as human beings, to making some sensible exceptions to our conversion to the metric system.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on this bill in spite of the fact that metrication now seems firmly on the road to being established in this country, and the fact that any debate at this point is more or less superfluous. Metrication is pretty well a fait accompli and we only have the trimmings to put in place.
What disturbs most Canadians is the fact that they have had very little to say about metrication or the implementation thereof. This was alluded to by my colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and my good friend the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). One reason is that the decision to proceed with the metric conversion program has been essentially by government decree. As such, it has been imposed upon Canadians in a rather arbitrary manner. Hon. members will recall that the principle of metrication was brought forth in a form of resolution, not a piece of legislation.
I want to make reference to the well-reasoned and rational approach to this piece of legislation by my colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain who placed on the record in a very articulate way some of the very serious shortcomings this legislation will impose upon the producers of western Canada and, indeed, the agricultural industry as a whole.
This bill is a sort of omnibus bill. It sets out to amend some nine different existing statutes, all aimed at facilitating the metric conversion process. I understand there will be something in the order of 81 more statutes which will have to be amended in order to accommodate the metric system.
I want to touch briefly on three different areas. First, I want to comment on the statements made by the minister respon-

sible for this legislation upon introduction of the bill. Second, I want to deal briefly with the impact of metrication upon the consumer. Finally, I want to deal with the impact of this piece of legislation and, in fact, the whole metric system, upon the agricultural sector.
In his address to this House when introducing this bill, the minister stated that the United States, our biggest trading partner-indeed, the largest trading partners in the world are the United States and Canada-is proceeding very rapidly with its program of metric conversion. I take issue with that statement. From my examination of the subject and from reading some of the debates before Congress and some of the American press, it does not seem as though the United States is proceeding very rapidly. My understanding is that they are still considering the pros and cons of the metric system and have been doing so since 1790. They still have a great deal of ambivalence toward this system. My conclusion is that their approach to metrication is something less than aggressive. In other words, they are not proceeding with this "go for broke" attitude as we are in this country.
It is interesting to note a survey conducted by the National Federation of Independent Business, a very large, independent business organization which has representatives in every part of the United States, some 400,000 members. The survey revealed that their membership was pretty well split on whether America should go with metric. At best, it seems very unlikely that total conversion will ever be a reality in the United States of America.
Many are concerned that conversion will endanger American jobs by making the U.S. more vulnerable to imports. Many workers have pointed out that they will reluctantly take early retirement rather than learn the new system. Farmers will never be ardent advocates of the metric system because of its cost and inconvenience with relatively no advantage. With this background, and having regard to this reaction and attitude toward the metric system-and, I might say, the lack of any broad support-the United States has opted for a cautious, rational plan in the conversion process without any compulsory features such as we see in our program. They have opted for a voluntary conversion program. This is alluded to in many articles which I have examined over the course of the past couple of weeks. For example, the Wall Street Journal of August 20, 1976, states as follows:
Last November a divided Congress shied away from mandating that the United States switch to the metric system of measurement, compromising instead on a national board to co-ordinate voluntary conversion.
In this way, the metric system will proceed in an orderly and rational manner. It will be imposed as industry becomes ready for it, and not before. In that connection, it is obvious that in the United States it is industry rather than the government which has been the leader. Some of the largest industrial concerns, particularly those engaged in multinational activity, have been leaders in the conversion process. Naturally, when they embark upon conversion their suppliers have to follow suit. The program is being implemented in an orderly manner with the minimum amount of disruption and economic impact.
January 26, 1977

There does not seem to be the compulsion in the United States which we have associated with this program in Canada. Persuasion, yes, but compulsion, no. I presume the multinational corporations in the United States are leaders in the conversion program because they are probably in the best position to pass along the cost involved in the form of higher prices to the consumer. Let there be no mistake; the consumer will ultimately bear the cost of metric conversion. No one has yet produced to me one scintilla of evidence that the metric system will benefit consumers. I have yet to see any cost analysis done in that connection.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext: What is a scintilla?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
The cost of conversion remains a highly significant factor. For example, General Motors which is a leader in the conversion process, has suggested that the cost will amount to about 1 per cent of gross sales over a period of ten years. But smaller firms, machine shops, small manufacturers and retailers suggest that their costs will escalate by as much as 20 per cent or 30 per cent in a period of a year or two during the firms' conversion process. These firms, however, state that they find no problem in adopting the system as far as cost is concerned, because they simply pass the cost along. One would think that in these times of inflationary pressure such increases would be regarded as a significant element in contributing to increased living costs and that we might contemplate slowing down the conversion process during a period of so-called restraint. I do not believe tha imposition of metric conversion is an effective way of fighting inflation. I repeat- the consumer will end up paying and he will be frustrated in the process.
I turn, now, to consider the impact this legislation will have upon the agricultural industry. I should point out, first of all, that farmers are not only producers; they are also major consumers. So this program will get them in the neck on both counts. While they constitute only 6 per cent of the national population, they spend more than $5 billion on materials and services associated with food production. No less than 45 per cent of Canada's gross national product is related to agriculture and allied industries.
As I stated earlier, and as explained by industry spokesmen both in Canada and the United States, the cost of conversion will merely be passed on, and to this extent farmers, as consumers, will be faced with increased costs. But there is an essential difference. Farmers do not enjoy the luxury of being able to pass on additional costs to consumers at will. They have to take what the market gives them. So we can expect the bulk of the conversion cost as it relates to agriculture to come out of the pocket of the farmer. If we consider the net farm income picture, which shows that in 1976 income was down by some 16 per cent compared to 1975-and net income for 1977 is expected to be below that for 1973-we cannot expect producers to be very enthusiastic about the prospects of additional costs associated with metrication.
Metric System
In addition to the element of cost, there is bound to be a great deal of inconvenience and confusion. We have come a long way in agriculture in terms of the standardization of repair parts-bearings, chains, hoses, and things of that nature. The advent of the metric system simply harms that trend. New tools will be required. The service industry, an important component of the agriculture industry, will be seriously affected. Inconvenience and confusion will be impossible to avoid, yet they are not accompanied by a single assurance of ultimate benefit to the agricultural industry either in the short or the long-term.
The minister told us that most of the farm organizations had endorsed metrication. This is surprising to me, because when those of us who represent rural constituencies talk to our constituents we find that people at the grass roots show little enthusiasm for the program. I would suspect that the government has consulted only the leaders of farm organizations and that those leaders have failed adequately to canvass their membership. Anyway, to judge from the evidence I have received, they certainly could not have consulted the producers.
The United States farm bureau, which is the largest farm organization in America, said in 1975 that adoption of the metric system did not have very high priority among its leaders. As far as the Canadian producer is concerned, it seems to me that on the international market we have been doing quite well in selling our grain to the elevator in bushels which are later converted into metric tons for sale abroad. The United States has also been doing quite well. The fact is that when customers need our grain they will buy it whether it is in bushels, pints or litres. The farmers, as I have pointed out, will be strangled with the cost of changes which will have to be made in the elevator system, such as scales modifications, with no significant benefit to them.
The other point I want to make is that the report on metric conversion and the grain market issued by the Canadian Livestock Feed Board points out that while we in Canada are going to convert from bushels to tonnes, the Chicago board of trade, with which we compete and with which we compare prices, will be continuing for some years using the Imperial measurement system. Therefore, this will again create confusion and additional cost. The grain transport industry, we are told, will continue for years under the present system. That point is also made in this publication. The report reads in part:
The grain transport industry will continue to use the present system for some years yet. No official date has been set for the rail and road transport systems to go metric in freight rate quotations.
So we will have a situation where trucks that come to the elevators will be weighed using the Imperial system of measurement, which will be converted to metric for payment and storage purposes and then will have to be converted back to the Imperial measure to accommodate our rail transportation system. It seems like a lot of extra work and a lot of bungling.

There may even be another bill.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
My colleague says there may be another bill. In the transportation field I have already pointed out that the changes are not due to take place for many years. It could be five, ten or two years. It was pointed out earlier that the knowledge producers have gained in terms of using the descriptions and the cliches is all part and parcel of the tools and culture of the trade. This knowledge will now all become essentially redundant.
Some 40 pages of documentation will require study on the part of elevator agents. They have been going to school in order to become proficient in the metric system. One really must ask who is going to gain. As my colleague pointed out, it certainly will not be the producer. If anyone, it will be those associated with the grain trade. I do not think we need go as far as converting bushels to tonnes. We have done well in the past selling bushels to the elevators, using metric tonnes in the international marketplace.
This leads me to another point, and that is the conversion of acres to hectares. Anyone who has lived in the west will know at a glance that this proposed conversion will be very serious in terms of geography, tradition and, indeed, our culture. It has been pointed out by my friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) that it will be a tremendous task to record land descriptions and make the necessary legal adjustments in registering land.
In that connection it is interesting to note, on examining the testimony given before the Congressional Senate committee in 1975, that the United States has made a firm commitment not to proceed with the conversion from acres to hectares, and I think this is a very important precedent which we should consider during the processing of this piece of legislation. It seems to me that if use of the acre is realistic in the United States, it certainly should be realistic in this country. If we convert to the hectare and the United States stays with the acre, then in terms of comparison and in terms of dealing with our great agricultural neighbour to the south we will be at a disadvantage. I would urge, as other speakers have, that the minister seriously reconsider the change from bushels to tonnes and from acres to hectares. I think we should provide this added flexibility in this legislation to accommodate a very important industry in this country, one which represents a very important economic sector of Canada. I do not think that the average farmer has really sensed the significance of metric conversion. When he wakes up and finds out just what it all means, Mr. Speaker, he is going to be very, very angry and disappointed.
While the metric system may dominate the world, there are still a number of valid exceptions in those countries that have adopted the metric system. For example, I understand that while Sweden uses the metric system, use is made of inches and feet in the construction of homes and in the lumber industry. I understand, as well, that in South America measures of pipe and lumber are still those of the Imperial system. I wonder, for example, what will happen in the aviation field, which essentially is an international field. Will it convert, or become one of the exceptions as well?

It seems to me that if we are interested in practicality and in common sense, we should give this measure further thought. I suggest that if we fail to do so, when the full impact of this legislation becomes known to the farmers the fat will really hit the fire and we will hear a lot of resentment of, and opposition to, the metric system. I hope that in the course of this debate the minister will seriously consider some of the very realistic and positive suggestions that have been advanced.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for an opportunity to say a few words in this discussion with respect to metric conversion in Canada. I will direct my remarks particularly to an area of great importance to my part of Canada, the grains industry with which Bill C-23 is largely concerned.
Change is always difficult to accept, especially when it affects important aspects of our daily living and our ways of earning a livelihood. People, quite naturally, develop a very strong attachment to familiar things and processes and there is predictable reluctance to something different. The metric conversion process is a classic example of this. Because of the magnitude of the change which is involved in this process and the impact which it will have upon people involved in the grains industry, particularly farmers, I am naturally concerned about the proposals contained in Bill C-23, and believe it is absolutely essential that the facts of this matter be clearly understood.
I want to deal with a few of the aspects of metric conversion affecting grain which may not be fully appreciated but upon the basis of which I believe this measure is not only supportable but is also in the best long-run interests of all segments of the grains industry, including producers in the prairie region. First, it should be noted that this change has a broad and virtually unanimous base of support in the farm community.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members opposite suggest that consultation with farmers is required. Without any suggestion or encouragement on their part, I spent a great deal of time not only during the Christmas recess but before, talking with farmers in my area about this proposal before I finally made up my mind on the subject. I did not find the degree of antagonism which they perhaps see, or perhaps it would be more proper to say that they would like to see and would like to foment.
As I was saying, this measure has a very broad and virtually unanimous base of support in the organized farming community. In the first place, I would point to the remarks of the

minister responsible for small business who is handling this bill for the government, who on December 21 of last year, at page 2230 of Hansard is reported as indicating that metric conversion in the grains industry has the active support of organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, the Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta Wheat Pools and the United Grain Growers. All of these are direct producer or producer-owned organizations and they are most anxious to see this resolution in place by February 1, 1977. Many of them, indeed, have made vigorous representations in this respect.
It is important, as well, to note the vehicle which has been utilized by the grains industry to deal with the process of conversion. I refer to the hardworking and longstanding metric conversion committee of the Canada Grains Council under the chairmanship of Mr. Earl Baxter, a well-known and widely-respected grain man. The membership of the council has been involved very directly in the positive work of that council's committee. That membership includes 28 separate firms and organizations associated with grain production, marketing, transportation and handling across Canada, many of them based in western Canada.
I will not take the time of the House to run through the full list of groups in the council, nor will I name at this time the very distinguished list of officers and directors of the council. I would simply point to the involvement of such organizations as the Canadian Seed Growers Association, the Hudson Bay Route Association, the Manitoba Farm Business Association, the Palliser Wheat Growers Association, the Rapeseed Association of Canada, the Union of Manitoba Municipalities and the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, and so on; and those are in addition to the CFA and UGG and others which were mentioned before. These are groups and organizations which form an active working base of the Canada Grains Council Committee.
I should also point out another interesting and important point which demonstrates the kind of support for metric conversion among western grain organizations and producer groups. While certain of these groups have, for their own reasons, withdrawn from the Canada Grains Council in other respects-and here I refer to the three prairie pools which indicate a very large farm membership including a large majority of prairie producers-these organizations have, nonetheless, participated fully in the metric work of the Canada Grains Council committee, despite the fact they have withdrawn from the council for other purposes. I think that is a significant point in demonstrating an important basis of support for the thrust of what is proposed in Bill C-23.
Let me now, Mr. Speaker, make a second general point which relates to what is going on in this connection in the United States. No doubt we in Canada, as others have pointed out, are ahead in this regard. We are years behind the rest of the industrialized world, but we are somewhat ahead of the United States. The conversion process is going on there as well, but in that country it is not yet as far advanced as it is in Canada.
Metric System
The general impression of many people closely involved with Canadian agriculture, and particularly with grain, is that there is no question about the United States intention of converting and the likelihood that it will be moving at an accelerated pace. Indeed, if you look at developments in the United States with respect to metric conversion in the last year to 18 months, you can see that acceleration beginning to develop, compared, for example, to what was happening two, three or four years ago. As well, for comparison purposes it is important to remember that the general commitment in Canada to conversion took place at least six years ago. It is obviously important for Canada to be slightly ahead in this connection, and not slightly behind. Therefore, I would suggest that the order of things is correct in this regard.
I want to deal, as well, with the question of cost, which has been mentioned, or more particularly with cost savings. A lot of people have been skeptical about the matter. In response to that skepticism I have asked the committee of the Grains Council to demonstrate clearly where the cost savings are, and it has produced a detailed analysis which indicates an annual saving to the grains industry in the order of $1 million. Over the long term I suggest that is, indeed, a significant saving. It is of a magnitude that should seriously be considered by those who would oppose this particular development.
Having said all that, may I clearly express my concern, which I share with my colleague the hon. member for Bat-tleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) and, more importantly, with farmers about the impact of this change. I think the minister responsible for this measure is also sensitive to these concerns. I was glad to hear members opposite today, like the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), express clear support for the principles involved in our conversion to the metric system. I was concerned that we might be up against a stone wall over there in this respect, but I see that is not, in fact, the case. I am grateful for that degree of receptivity and I, for one, am prepared to examine all suggestions for ameliorating any negative consequences which could possibly result from the conversion process. Indeed, I have been active in making suggestions in this direction to the minister and government officials involved.
In particular, I agree with the general suggestion about a thorough and effective educational program for everyone affected in the context of Bill C-23, but particularly for farmers. I also agree with the idea of as gradual a conversion process as seems reasonably feasible, given the state of developments at the present moment. In that context we have to remember the very significant work that has already been done by the Canada Grains Council committee, work that now stretches back over the better part of six or seven years and which has had a great deal of support and active involvement from the farming community across Canada, particularly the grain industry in the west.
I believe that on this side there is a willingness to hear and understand the concerns which have not only been expressed today and on other occasions when we have debated this

January 26, 1977
Metric System
measure but have been expressed in other places and at other times by farmers in particular. I think there is still, as well, a willingness to respond in a sensitive and sensible way. I will be active in working with the responsible minister in this connection and I hope that members on all sides of this House will adopt the same kind of positive approach to this very difficult and delicate issue which can, I think, by the admission of all involved-whether they may in the short-term oppose or support it-work in the best interests of all of Canada, including the grains industry.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a little difficult to find new things to say on this subject after the number of speeches that have already been made, but I would like to add a few comments in order to voice my concerns and reservations about the proposal. We all accept the fact that many eminent individuals, institutions and organizations have urged at one time or another that a system common to the whole world in respect of weights and measures should be adopted. Perhaps one can think of many advantages when looking at this from a theoretical point of view. It is perhaps fair to say that no one has strongly challenged the benefits that may be achieved by a system which is similar or the same throughout the world.
One could make some suggestions with regard to practical considerations. Theoretically, one could accept easily enough that there should be advantages if everybody talked the same language in so far as weights and measures are concerned, but I suggest that practical considerations make it rather impractical to hope that such can be achieved without great difficulty in many areas of Canadian life.
The area I would like to stress is the psychological effect on people; if nothing else, the fear of the unknown, so to speak. There is a fear of being taken out of a system with which everyone is familiar and being cast into an unknown situation. There may be some psychological disadvantages resulting from being tossed into an unknown world and out of the area where one feels comfortable. It has been mentioned that weights and measures in pounds, inches and so on have indeed become part of our very culture and part of the custom and way of life we enjoy.
I suppose to illustrate one might say that it would be very useful if in this world everybody spoke the same language. No doubt there would be advantages in terms of communication between people. Perhaps that could even prevent wars, and it certainly would contribute to greater understanding between people and nations. However, that is not being done. Nobody is promoting very seriously the idea that because there are so many advantages all nations should abandon their native tongues and accept some common language which everybody in the world could speak.
The reasons are obvious. One reason is that people have a psychological attachment to the language with which they have been living all their lives and to which they are accustomed. There is a psychological attachment to the culture they

have enjoyed, so they simply refuse, in spite of a long list of advantages which I am sure anybody could envisage, to adopt a common language the world over. I think that same argument, perhaps less forcibly, applies in so far as trying to accept or impose on the world a common system of weights and measures.
I am not convinced that the scientific superiority which it is theorized would occur from this conversion would indeed be an advantage or should, indeed, prevail over the established commercial customs and practices with which we are all familiar; and if there is a scientific superiority of some sort which would prevail, the government has been very weak in making the case and many questions remain unanswered.
We have not seen any kind of cost projection in Canada. We have seen some studies from the United States, but we have not seen any studies here as to what the long-range benefits might be. There has not been a cost-benefit study done weighing the benefits against the disadvantages or weighing the disadvantages over whatever benefits might occur in the long run. We know from American studies that the Americans expect their metrification to cost somewhere around $50 billion. If we calculate, on the ratio basis, their population to ours, I suppose it would be safe to assume that the cost to Canada would be somewhere in the vicinity of $5 billion. We have to ask ourselves, from the economic point of view, whether today, when Canada is experiencing severe inflation and severe difficulty with its economy, we should be pushing so fast and so hard to impose this additional $5 billion price tag on the people of Canada.
Of course, it will be the people of Canada who will be paying, not this government nor any of the hon. members opposite who have spoken and who are so convinced that we must rush into this and complete the conversion by 1980. I think it has to be shown that a balanced study of some kind has been carried out with regard to the long-term benefits as opposed to whatever short-term expediency might be envisaged by the government in jumping into this change.
In deciding to proceed with this metrification program, what costs must be considered? I submit that the list is a very long one. In terms of cost this conversion will affect virtually every citizen of the country. The people who are involved in the manufacturing industry seem to be convinced that this is a good thing. I submit perhaps that they are the only ones who are. Perhaps only those in the manufacturing sector of our economy can show clearly that there will be some sort of advantage, the advantage being that their products will be more easily interchangeable and perhaps, therefore, more easily exported to other countries of the world where the metric system is already in effect.
However, we must think of the machinery and tools of production which must be changed. If we are talking about agriculture, new scales in grain elevators will be required. At service stations new gas pumps with new numbers will be required. At home new gas meters and water meters will be required. On highways there will need to be new highway signs. Clothing manufacturers will need to use new clothing
January 26, 1977

dimensions. The construction industry will require new plans and specifications and will have to operate under different systems. All these things add very substantially to the cost of production. I submit that in view of those costs at a time when we are trying to increase our productivity-and the government admits that is the most successful way of beating inflation in the long run-we will wind up with a slowdown in productivity while everybody tries to adjust.
Just to give an example of the cost of machinery, a meatpacking plant in my constituency which does a moderate business estimates that just to change the scales and other machines the plant is looking at a price tag of about $3,000. Perhaps to a government which deals with billions of dollars that does not sound like very much, but to a small business operation it can be a significant amount.
There are a whole bunch of other considerations which we call intangibles. We will have to learn new words and how to use them. We will have to try to get our brains adjusted to new numbers. If a person is running a lumber yard and somebody comes to his place of business and asks for 5.08 x 10.15, 305 centimetres long, what do hon. members think he will be asking for? Suppose he asks for a nail 6.349 centimetres long. What should he be given? We will be ordering sheets of plywood 1.22 x 2.43 metres. All these are simply figures-but they just do not register.
I see that my hon. friend who used to be an Edmonton Eskimo has stepped out of the House temporarily, but when I was listening to the other debaters I looked at him and thought of Miss Edmonton Eskimo. When we recall that last year's Miss Edmonton Eskimo's qualifications were 36-24-36, that has some immediate impact on the minds of Canadians. If her qualifications were expressed as 92-61-92, I am afraid that the impact would be far different and less meaningful.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC MEASUREMENT
speechtext:
I am saying this to try to emphasize the disruption which will occur to the registering processes in people's brains which have been imprinted there during the course of the experiences of their lifetimes. Suddenly to take this, to scrap it all and try to re-educate everybody is totally unrealistic. It just cannot be done. I practiced medicine before I came into politics. Hospitals converted a long time ago, but when I was in medical school-which is not that long ago; I graduated in 1960-we still thought of temperatures in terms of Fahrenheit. After, metrification, when nurses phoned me to tell me that a child's temperature was 38 degrees, I always automatically asked her to tell me what that was in Fahrenheit. They had a chart with Centigrade on one side and Fahrenheit on the other. Thirty-eight degrees does not register on my brain, and I submit that this is a problem which is common to all aspects of Canadian life. When someone is given a number from another system, it does not register. That person does not know for sure what it means, so we wind up with the possibility of all kinds of technical people making all kinds of mistakes and, indeed, some of those mistakes could be very serious.
Metric System
I have mentioned already that during the process of trying to learn new measurements there is bound to be a slowdown in production. You can take the example of a mechanic working on a motor. He sees a nut of a certain size and he automatically reaches for the right wrench. If you give him a metric nut- no pun intended on any member on the other side of the House-he has to examine all his wrenches to select the one which fits that nut, and it is no longer automatic. The effect is that he becomes less productive; it takes him longer to repair the motor because he has to spend time selecting his wrenches, something which was automatic before.
We have to ask ourselves this question. Because of this loss of experience, so to speak, how many mistakes will be made in industry, science, medicine, in the bakery or in the kitchen? The housewife will no longer be able to use her cook book. She is familiar with a cupful as a measurement, but the new directions will be in millilitres. This should not be taken as a reflection on housewives, but they will be at least as confused any anyone else trying to get used to this new system.
The question, then, is: When you are looking at the price-tag of metrification, how do you calculate the cost of psychological factors, the intangible discomforts which we will have to face?
I submit it is almost impossible to put a price-tag on these intangible but great discomforts, and the very roots of our thinking will be taxed and shaken.
I would be inclined to agree with the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) that the world is moving in that direction and indeed that many countries in the world are using the metric system. But if we are to accept it, we should take a little more time and perhaps begin in the schools, in grade one, to teach the system to the children first. In a generation or so the changeover will be very simple, almost automatic. But we are rushing to complete it by 1980 and because of that all kinds of unnecessary new stresses are being placed on the minds of Canadians.
I think it would be useful to look at this question from many points of view. One of them is that there may be an advantage in converting to the metric system because anyone who uses machinery of a certain type will have to change over and buy new machinery and different kinds of equipment. So there will be a sudden stimulus in the manufacturing sector to produce new equipment which will be required. Perhaps this is an advantage at a time of high unemployment, but the disadvantages are indeed very great.
A proper profit and loss assessment of this proposal has never been made in the Canadian context. I have already touched on the reasons in part, namely, that the concept of a simple addition of the benefits which may occur, or of the greater cost which may be involved, is simply not feasible because the intangibles are virtually impossible to assess. Some attempts have been made in the United States, for example, to communicate with industry, with labour, with agriculture and with scientific groups, asking each one of them to outline what they construe to be the benefits and the disadvantages in terms of cost. From what I can gather, the manufacturing sector

Metric System
thought there might be advantages. But the advantages of this system are not obvious, and the disadvantages in the immediate future can readily be seen because it is in the immediate future that the conversion and the added expense have to take place. The advantages will not be visible for a number of years. The estimates for recovery of the cost in the manufacturing sector show that recovery will take place only after about 15 years.
In agriculture, for example, if it takes as long as 15 years to recover the cost of conversion to the metric system it is a long time. Many farmers do not have 15 years on a farm. The way things are today, with costs escalating beyond belief, this added cost could well be the last straw that breaks the camel's back and drives an ever greater number of farmers off the land into another area where the net income is much more attractive.
Let us consider the construction industry and how it will be affected. Today everyone is trained in the system of Imperial weights and measures. I am speaking of planners and architects who know what the standards specifications are in feet and inches when they measure plywood, windows, doors or door-frames. All these things are part of their existing knowledge. If you start measuring everything in centimetres it will cause mass confusion and require mass retraining. It is quite easy to see that the labourer's costs will be very great. He will have to buy new tools. If he works for an employer, his tools might be bought for him, but if he is self-employed he has no such option. Then there is the question as to who will bear the cost of retraining.
Coming back to what I said before, metrication means, in effect, loss of experience. With one fell swoop you take an experienced mechanic and make him inexperienced because he has to learn a new system. His productivity will decline because of his loss of experience in his trade. What is the dollar value of that, and who will absorb it?
I wanted to make reference to non-manufacturing businesses, to the service industry. From all the studies I was able to make it is obvious that no great advantages will accrue to the restaurants. The owner will be at a disadvantage because he will have to buy new tools, new scales, and so on. In no way will that increase his productivity or his return. He might have to retrain his cooks and kitchen help to think metric, but he will not thereby increase their productivity. You cannot bake any more pies by using centimetres. So in the service industry there will certainly be added costs but no visible advantages.
Let us consider the educational system. There are all kinds of things to consider there. If you talk to the chairman of any school board in this country and ask him how his budget stands, virtually all of them will tell you that their budget is grossly overstrained because of rising costs. However, all the textbooks will have to be converted; and who will absorb the cost of rewriting the textbooks? In the area of education there is clearly an advantage when teaching mathematics to children. We all accept the fact that it is easier to learn the concept of decimals and the metric system than the old system.

But that is overbalanced by the cost of converting textbooks and all the equipment used in schools.
I should like now to touch on the subject of agriculture, Mr. Speaker. This is an area of primary production where the costs are very obvious. They are variable, but I think substantial in terms of making alterations to machinery and so forth. There are many disadvantages in the area of agriculture, but no advantages to be seen regarding productivity. So many tons per hectare of wheat does not bring about higher productivity than under the old system. If you give a horse two kilograms of oats instead of half a gallon, the horse is not really going to eat any less; in order to keep going he will require the usual amount. If you measure the milk given by a cow in litres, it is not going to give any more milk than if you measure it in quarts. From the point of view of the farmer there is little to be gained and a lot to be lost in addition to the intangible, psychological disturbances to which I have already referred.
I should like to make a brief reference to civil aviation, Mr. Speaker. It is very important in my constituency which covers one-quarter of the province of Alberta. Charter airlines flourish in the northern regions and, indeed, air is the only practical way to travel. We have to think of the safety factor here. At present a runway is so many feet long or wide and the wind so many nautical miles per hour. But suddenly pilots are being told about metres of ground ahead and that they are so many metres from the end of the runway. Their safety could be jeopardized by this in the same way as in the French-English dispute of the air controllers who want to use their own language. Some people say this would not be safe because of the possibility of mistakes. The same applies to measurements of speed, elevation or dimensions of the runway, and so on.
All these things are presently communicated by the old system. It seems to me there is great possibility of a decrease in the safety of civil aviation unless a vigorous effort is made to retrain the people concerned into thinking metric. Air controllers would have to be retrained, and we members may have to stay here all the time because we will be afraid to travel to our constituencies in case the air controllers are not able to make the necessary calculations.
I should like to quote from a New York Times article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of December 20, 1975, which describes what is taking place in the field of civil aviation with regard to metrification. The article reads:
Civil aviation is one field where no one is hurrying to switch to metric, because in no other area is safety so dependent upon measurement. The foot, pound and nautical mile system is used in all but communist countries for runway dimensions, in calculating distances and altitudes, for visibility and pressure gauges and in some thermometers.
We have heard nothing from the other side about this particular problem. With that, Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks and hope that somebody over there was listening and will provide answers to these questions before we rush this bill through the House.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose if the Liberal party wanted a good example of why their popularity has been sagging lately, this would be as good a place as any to start-their method of introducing metrication. Everyone I have spoken to has some doubts about it. I do not know where the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) has been, because in my long experience of dealing with farmers, no matter from what part of the country, I find they usually speak the same language. But the language I heard when I was out west in the last few weeks apparently was entirely different from the language the hon. member for Assiniboia would have the House and the country believe they are speaking.
A lot of reservation was expressed about this subject both in my constituency and outside, and I cannot believe the situation is any different in his constituency. Perhaps he has trained some of his supporters to accept that any policy enunciated by the Liberal party has to be good for the country. Perhaps they bow in subservience to him and do not register dissatisfaction because that might not be popular with the government. If ever the government needed friends, it is now; so this might be the time for them to come forward and then the government can downplay the amount of criticism they are getting about this measure.
I hear people say this is another case of the east shoving something down the throat of the west. That is bad enough, but I also hear the comment-which will perhaps affect members here more than the comment about the east dominating the west-that because the metric system is perhaps more synonymous with the French, that is why they are introducing it. These are comments I have heard, that perhaps it is a French Canadian who decided it is good for us, so we will have to proceed with it.

I am simply registering a comment I have heard. If it excites the hon. member, perhaps he should understand there is another part of this country. He should perhaps understand that there are members who do not represent manufacturing areas, and he should understand that this bill will only really benefit manufacturers. It does not really matter to the manufacturer, in terms of total exports, whether you read the temperature in Celsius or in Fahrenheit. A lot of people comment on that, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps it is not a complicated matter to measure degrees of frost, but a lot of people say the other system was better because they had a greater variation. From minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit to 108 degrees Fahrenheit there is a variation of 150 degrees, but from minus 40 degrees Celsius to 37 degrees Celsius there is only an 80-degree variation. What annoys a lot of farmers is that the manufacturers have said, "This is good for us" and have sold the government on the idea.
True, a large portion of the world is under the metric system, but in this country farmers, consumers and even
Metric System
manufacturers have been used to dealing with equipment of standard sizes. What will you do in future if you want to replace the old hubcaps on your car? Will the manufacturer have them in the right size? Remember, not all people buy brand new cars. What will happen when you want a new windshield but the manufacturers do not make them in the old, standard sizes? You couldn't replace it by taking an old windshield from another car. The government is oblivious to our concerns. Manufacturers say that the new system will be good for them but never mind the cost to the consumer, and the government has gone along with them.
Unfortunately, debate at this stage is useless. However, useless as it may be, we as members have the right to register our protests. We ought to have registered them five, six or seven years ago when the idea was first submitted. Perhaps the government would have approached conversion differently if we had made our views known. Perhaps it would have got some sort of guarantee from manufacturers with regard to standardization of parts. That would have been better than having this new system shoved down our throats. What happens when you want to buy a tire? Today you ask a tire dealer, "What is the size of that tire?" and he will say, "It is a G-78," or something like that. I can understand what one means when he talks of a 7.50 x 15, or 8.00 x 15, or even 8.25 x 15 tire, but I do not understand what is meant by a G-78 or an H-78 or J-78. Not only can the tire dealer not tell you anything about it, but the salesman is no help. So what is the result? There is utter confusion. This is just another case of planned obsolescence without beneficial result.
We have been told to speed passage of this bill because the grains industry needs it. I am not so sure about that. There was a sign on an elevator back home saying that the elevator was to be closed as of January 31 in order to convert to the metric system. Obviously, the operator intended to close and convert; he had all the forms prepared and he was getting ready to convert. Therefore, whether we pass this bill or not, he will have to convert to the new system. What is he to do if we do not pass this bill? Throw away all those forms?
There is no point in this exercise. The Liberal party suddenly realized that conversion was being criticized. What has it done? It has treated this question as it treated bilingualism and said, "This is good for the country. You must have it." When it implemented its bilingual policy it sent civil servants only two years from retirement for language training. It sent them on total immersion courses. The program cost millions of dollars, but cost was not a factor. Now we find that the program is not working. The government is using the same approach with the present measure.
Some members have already alluded to the confusion which will be created in the minds of farmers. For instance, some of our farm drills are spaced six or seven inches apart. If you want to test the accuracy of your drill, you know that you will plant so many kernels after you move so many feet. Now you are about to confuse the farmer by introducing variations.
Take the case of rapeseed. You must be most accurate when planting rapeseed; perhaps you need not be quite so accurate

January 26, 1977
Metric System
with other grains. Mistakes can be costly. Farmers have talked to me about their sprayers. The sprayer jets are spaced 20 inches apart. Farmers know their height, they know the volume of the sprayer tanks and they know how much spray they should be using for a given area. If you put too much in, you will burn the crop; but if you put too little in, it is a waste of time. Therefore, you must be accurate. If you make mistakes, you end up losing money. With the unfamiliar metric system this will happen.
Has the government received any assurance from manufacturers that replacement parts will be readily available in years to come? Much farm equipment will still be good for many years to come. I suspect that the answer is no, you will have to scrap the whole machine for want of a part. I have seen it happen. I remember what happened to imported German tractors which were used out west. Within two years those tractors were sitting in the bush, rotting because you could not buy replacement parts for them. I remember the Long tractor which came on the market about 25 years ago. I don't know who Mr. Long was; I never heard of him before or after. All I know is that some farmers were sucked in to buying that machine. It went off the market and farmers lost money. Has the government considered this aspect, or does it not care?
Obviously, the government thinks this is good for us. Mr. Speaker, the bulk of our exports, approximately 70 per cent, go to the United States. The government tells us that we are going to break into the world market. Well, you are not going to break into the world market simply by converting. Actually, we stand a good chance of losing our existing United States market, and I will tell you why. The Americans do not have to buy from us. They can manufacture their own materials and are already doing so. They are going slowly with their conversion. They may consider it worth their while to spend a little more money and buy from sources other than Canada. At least they will be assured of getting standardized parts. Many customers in the Unites States will think twice before buying from Canada.
What are we doing? We are to be in the forefront of a change. This is to be a great step forward. I do not know how many farm units or farm orgnizations were consulted, but I do know that they did not have many meetings across the country or, if people from those organizations attended the meetings, they did not understand what they were all about. I can tell you that many did not understand what was going on. Therefore, how could they explain it to others?
The government too, has encountered problems. But did any representative of the minister go out to these organizations and try to explain the ramifications of the programs, its pros and cons? Not in this case. If there was ever an occasion when we needed an educational program, this was it. It is not so much that people cannot be retrained, because I am sure they can. We must give them time and you must assure them that conversion will bring benefits. Out west our roads are spaced according to certain plans. Roads running north and south are one mile apart; roads running east and west are two miles apart. Try giving the minister directions, using the new system,

to get into a farmer's place. Instead of telling him to go so many miles east or west, you will tell him, "Go ten kilometres south, plus a little bit, one kilometre east, plus a little bit, then turn right and go five kilometres, plus a little bit." Where do you end up?

I was talking about the sprayer. The farmer does not want new equipment: he still wants to be sure that he is using a gallon, a half-gallon, a quart or a pint. He does not care what it states on the container; he intends to continue measuring in the way he has always done. Chances are that he will be right using the old method. The government system is like everything else: when the government suggests something is good for you, do the opposite and you are sure to come out on top.
I can assure the minister and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), who accepts this program with open arms, that I am getting an entirely different point of view. For example, those working in hospitals will have to use a new measurement for doses of medication. Some say they would rather quit than take the chance of giving someone the wrong amount of medication. This is not a laughing matter. It is said that they can be retrained, but the fact is these people are afraid to take on this responsibility. How can they be sure?
All this government has done is set a deadline. As far as the west is concerned, this system should have been started 70 years ago. At that time a lot of people came from Europe. They understood the metric system. It would have been a simple matter for this country to have accepted this system at that time. However, they were forced to learn a new system. Their children were trained in the new system. Now they have forgotten the old metric system. Had governments accepted the metric system at that time, there may not have been confusion with land surveys, and so on.
Possibly the minister does not have anything to do. For lack of something better to do he feels he should pilot a bill through the House. I will give him something to do. I suggest that he go to the drugstore to purchase a tube of shaving cream. There he will find at least three different measurements-ounces, millilitres and grammes. Without the aid of a computer let the minister figure out which is the better deal. I defy him to do that.
When you think you get a good deal shopping at a grocery store there is nothing worse than finding that two doors away the store has a much better deal. This is how the housewife feels. Is the minister monitoring what is going on? I am sure he is not because it is too trivial. However, if enough of this is going on it will affect the total cost of production. That is what

this is all about. If the cost of production goes higher, how can you compete?
There was talk about the 2x4. An architect or engineer may be familiar with one system and then suddenly find himself having to use another system. This will necessitate checking and double-checking. Some architects charge a very stiff fee. If their staff drags simply because they want to be doubly sure rather than have an inaccurate calculation, who will pay? Imagine trying to estimate the cost of a project. If there are variations, who will take the blame? Obviously, the standard excuse will be that somewhere along the line somebody goofed.
No matter how you look at it, there is only benefit for the manufacturer. We have heard the one-sided argument that it is good for us, that it will be good for Canada. It has already been pointed out that grain will not be sold by the bushel. However, it will still be necessary to convert. Talk to the elevator agents. Boxcars will still be measured in terms of bushels. They will have to be converted, even with the new system.
There is no point trying to convince us that this system will be good. We do not want to be sheep, particularly if we have to be led by this government. Anything this government does must be checked and double-checked. That is one of the reasons it takes longer than is sometimes necessary to get legislation through.
